chunks.title: Pathophysiology and Diagnostic Criteria of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
chunks.source: American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care
chunks.citation: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2024, Diabetes Care 2024;47(Suppl. 1):S20–S42
chunks.text: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) is characterized by progressive loss of adequate beta-cell insulin secretion frequently on the background of insulin resistance in liver, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue. Diagnostic criteria for diabetes require one of the following confirmed by repeat testing in the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia: 1. Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) >= 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) after an 8-hour fast. 2. 2-hour plasma glucose >= 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) during a 75g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). 3. HbA1c >= 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) using an NGSP-certified assay. 4. Classic symptoms of hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis with a random plasma glucose >= 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L). Prediabetes is defined as FPG 100-125 mg/dL (impaired fasting glucose) or 2-hour PG 140-199 mg/dL (impaired glucose tolerance) or HbA1c 5.7-6.4%.

chunks.title: Glycemic Targets and Individualization of HbA1c in T2DM
chunks.citation: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2024, Diabetes Care 2024;47(Suppl. 1):S111–S125
chunks.text: An HbA1c goal of < 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) is appropriate for many non-pregnant adult patients with Type 2 Diabetes to prevent or slow microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy). Stringent targets (< 6.5%) may be considered for younger patients with short diabetes duration, long life expectancy, and no significant cardiovascular disease if achievable without significant hypoglycemia or adverse treatment effects. Less stringent targets (< 8.0% or 8.5%) are indicated for patients with a history of severe hypoglycemia, limited life expectancy, advanced microvascular or macrovascular complications, extensive comorbid conditions, or long-standing diabetes difficult to control. HbA1c reflects average glycemia over approximately 90-120 days, weighted towards the preceding 30 days. Conditions that alter red blood cell turnover (hemoglobinopathies, severe anemia, hemodialysis) require plasma glucose or fructosamine evaluation.

chunks.title: Fasting and Postprandial Blood Glucose Monitoring & Targets
chunks.citation: WHO Package of Essential NCD Interventions 2023; ADA Standards of Care 2024, Section 6
chunks.text: Target preprandial (fasting) capillary blood glucose for non-pregnant adults with T2DM is 80–130 mg/dL (4.4–7.2 mmol/L). Peak postprandial capillary blood glucose (measured 1–2 hours after the start of a meal) target is < 180 mg/dL (< 10.0 mmol/L). Fasting hyperglycemia predominantly reflects excessive hepatic glucose output and basal insulin deficiency, whereas postprandial hyperglycemia reflects impaired first-phase insulin secretion and peripheral insulin resistance following carbohydrate ingestion. Marked discordance between HbA1c and fasting glucose often indicates postprandial glycemic excursions. Self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG) frequency should be tailored to medication regimen: higher frequency with insulin/secretagogues, and structured periodic testing for non-insulin regimens.

chunks.title: Routine Laboratory Testing Schedule for Type 2 Diabetes
chunks.source: Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) & ADA Standards
chunks.section: Comprehensive Medical Evaluation and Assessment of Comorbidities
chunks.citation: ICMR Guidelines for Management of Type 2 Diabetes 2023, Ch. 3; ADA Standards 2024, Section 4
chunks.text: Routine laboratory monitoring for T2DM patients includes: 1. HbA1c testing at least twice yearly in patients meeting glycemic goals and stable regimens; quarterly in patients whose therapy has changed or who are not meeting goals. 2. Serum creatinine and calculated estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR) at least annually (every 3–6 months if eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73m2). 3. Spot urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) annually to detect early diabetic kidney disease. 4. Fasting lipid panel (Total cholesterol, LDL-C, HDL-C, Triglycerides) annually, or every 4-12 weeks following initiation or adjustment of lipid-lowering therapy. 5. Liver function enzymes (AST, ALT) annually, especially given high prevalence of Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatohepatitis (MASH). 6. Serum potassium and electrolytes when prescribed ACE inhibitors, ARBs, SGLT2 inhibitors, or diuretics.

chunks.title: Metformin Pharmacology, Efficacy, and Dosing Guidelines
chunks.citation: DailyMed Metformin Hydrochloride Prescribing Information; ADA Standards of Care 2024, Section 9
chunks.text: Metformin (biguanide class) decreases hepatic glucose production, decreases intestinal absorption of glucose, and improves insulin sensitivity by increasing peripheral glucose uptake and utilization. Typical starting dose is 500 mg once or twice daily with meals, titrated weekly to a target dose of 1000 mg twice daily (or 2000 mg extended release once daily). Expected HbA1c reduction is approximately 1.0% to 1.5%. Metformin is weight-neutral or promotes modest weight loss and does not cause hypoglycemia as monotherapy. Common adverse reactions include gastrointestinal symptoms (diarrhea, nausea, abdominal discomfort), which can be mitigated by taking doses with meals and gradual titration. Long-term use is associated with biochemical vitamin B12 deficiency; periodic monitoring of B12 levels is recommended, especially in patients with anemia or peripheral neuropathy.

chunks.title: SGLT2 Inhibitors (Empagliflozin, Dapagliflozin, Canagliflozin) in T2DM
chunks.section: Cardiovascular and Renal Disease Risk Reduction
chunks.citation: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2024, Section 10; DailyMed Empagliflozin Package Insert
chunks.text: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors reduce renal glucose reabsorption in the proximal renal tubules, promoting urinary glucose excretion (glucosuria) independent of insulin secretion. Common agents: Empagliflozin (10-25 mg daily), Dapagliflozin (5-10 mg daily), Canagliflozin (100-300 mg daily). Key clinical benefits: significant reduction in heart failure hospitalizations, progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD), and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with established ASCVD or high risk. Glycemic efficacy decreases with declining renal function (minimal glucose lowering when eGFR < 45 mL/min/1.73m2), yet renoprotective and cardioreprotective benefits persist down to eGFR 20 mL/min/1.73m2. Adverse risks: mycotic genital infections, urinary tract infections, volume depletion, and rare euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (euDKA).

chunks.title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists (Semaglutide, Dulaglutide, Liraglutide) in T2DM
chunks.citation: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2024, Section 9 & 10; DailyMed Semaglutide Prescribing Information
chunks.text: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppress inappropriate glucagon secretion, slow gastric emptying, and promote satiety via central nervous system pathways. Substantial HbA1c reduction (1.0% to 2.0%) and robust weight loss (5% to 15%). Cardiovascular outcome trials demonstrate significant reduction in 3-point MACE (cardiovascular death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke) in patients with established ASCVD or high risk. Adverse effects are predominantly gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation), which attenuate over time. Black box warning: contraindicated in patients with personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2). Caution is advised in patients with pre-existing severe proliferative diabetic retinopathy or history of pancreatitis.

chunks.title: DPP-4 Inhibitors and Sulfonylureas in Type 2 Diabetes
chunks.citation: ICMR Guidelines for Management of T2DM 2023; DailyMed Sitagliptin and Glimepiride Prescribing Info
chunks.text: Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors (Sitagliptin, Linagliptin, Vildagliptin) prevent degradation of endogenous incretin hormones (GLP-1, GIP). Efficacy: modest HbA1c reduction (0.5%–0.8%). Well-tolerated, weight-neutral, negligible hypoglycemia risk as monotherapy. Linagliptin requires no renal dose adjustment; Sitagliptin requires dose adjustment according to eGFR. Sulfonylureas (Glimepiride, Glipizide, Gliclazide) stimulate beta-cell insulin secretion by closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels. Efficacy: rapid initial HbA1c reduction (1.0%–1.5%), but lack durability due to progressive beta-cell failure. Major limitations: substantial hypoglycemia risk (especially in elderly patients or kidney impairment) and modest weight gain (1.5–2.5 kg). Sulfonylureas should not be combined with meglitinides, and caution is mandatory when combining with insulin.

chunks.title: Renal Dosing Adjustments and Medication Safety Thresholds in T2DM
chunks.section: Safety, Renal Dosing, and Drug-Drug Interactions
chunks.citation: ADA Standards 2024, Section 11 (Chronic Kidney Disease); DailyMed Prescribing Alerts
chunks.text: Critical renal safety thresholds for antidiabetic medications: 1. Metformin: Measure eGFR prior to initiation. Safe to start if eGFR >= 45 mL/min/1.73m2. If eGFR is 30–44 mL/min/1.73m2, do not initiate; if already taking, max dose is 1000 mg/day with frequent renal monitoring. Contraindicated if eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73m2 due to risk of lactic acidosis. Withhold prior to iodinated radiocontrast procedures in patients with eGFR 30-60. 2. SGLT2 Inhibitors: Glycemic lowering declines below eGFR 45; can be continued for cardiorenal protection down to eGFR 20 mL/min/1.73m2 or dialysis. 3. GLP-1 RAs: Dulaglutide and subcutaneous Semaglutide do not require dose adjustment for renal impairment, but hydration must be maintained to prevent acute kidney injury from GI volume depletion. 4. Sulfonylureas: Prolonged half-life in renal impairment increases hypoglycemia risk; Glimepiride and Glyburide active metabolites accumulate; dose reduction or discontinuation required when eGFR < 45.

chunks.title: Adherence Evaluation, Clinical Inertia, and Behavioral Barriers
chunks.section: Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors and Well-being
chunks.citation: WHO Adherence to Long-Term Therapies: Evidence for Action; ADA Standards 2024, Section 5
chunks.text: Medication adherence in chronic Type 2 Diabetes is a critical determinant of glycemic stability and complication prevention. Non-adherence rates reach 30%–50% in long-term observational cohorts, contributing to pseudo-refractory hyperglycemia. Key barriers include: complex multi-dose schedules, gastrointestinal adverse effects (metformin, GLP-1 RAs), fear of hypoglycemia (insulin, sulfonylureas), medication cost, and health literacy limitations. Dataset considerations: Publicly available retrospective datasets typically record refill encounters or self-report proxies rather than electronic pill-bottle monitoring. Proportion of Days Covered (PDC) >= 80% is the accepted benchmark for adequate adherence when prescription refill claims are available. When refill intervals are incomplete, metrics must be classified as proxy or exploratory indicators rather than validated ground-truth adherence.

chunks.title: Medical Nutrition Therapy and Physical Activity for Type 2 Diabetes
chunks.source: ADA Standards of Care & ICMR Guidelines
chunks.citation: ADA Standards of Care 2024, Section 5; ICMR T2DM Guidelines 2023, Ch. 2
chunks.text: Lifestyle interventions form the cornerstone of T2DM management alongside pharmacotherapy: 1. Nutrition: Emphasize nutrient-dense, high-fiber eating patterns (Mediterranean, DASH, plant-forward diets). Reduce refined carbohydrates, sugar-sweetened beverages, and ultra-processed foods. Focus on consistent carbohydrate distribution. 2. Weight Management: A 5%–10% intentional weight reduction in overweight or obese patients produces clinically meaningful improvements in glycemic control, lipid profiles, and blood pressure. 3. Physical Activity: Non-pregnant adults should engage in at least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous aerobic activity weekly spread over at least 3 days, with no more than 2 consecutive days without exercise. Add 2–3 sessions of resistance exercise per week on non-consecutive days. 4. Sleep & Behavioral Health: Encourage 7–8 hours of uninterrupted sleep; screen for obstructive sleep apnea and diabetes distress.

chunks.title: Microvascular and Macrovascular Complication Screening in T2DM
chunks.citation: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2024, Section 11 & 12
chunks.text: Screening guidelines for T2DM chronic complications: 1. Retinopathy: Dilated, comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist at the time of T2DM diagnosis and annually thereafter (or every 2 years if exams are normal). 2. Diabetic Kidney Disease: Annual assessment of urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) and eGFR beginning at diagnosis. 3. Neuropathy: Annual screening for distal symmetric polyneuropathy using 10-g monofilament test, pinprick or temperature sensation, and ankle reflex testing. 4. Diabetic Foot: Comprehensive foot examination annually to identify ulceration, peripheral arterial disease, and loss of protective sensation. 5. Cardiovascular Disease: Regular assessment of cardiovascular risk factors (blood pressure >= 130/80 mmHg, dyslipidemia, smoking status, family history). ASCVD is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality.

chunks.title: Chronic Kidney Disease Staging, eGFR, and Albuminuria in T2DM
chunks.source: KDIGO 2023 Clinical Practice Guideline & ADA Standards
chunks.citation: KDIGO 2023 Diabetes Management in CKD; ADA Standards 2024, Section 11
chunks.text: Diabetic Kidney Disease (DKD) is staged based on estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR) and Urinary Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio (UACR): eGFR Categories (mL/min/1.73m2): - G1: >= 90 (Normal or high) - G2: 60–89 (Mildly decreased) - G3a: 45–59 (Mildly to moderately decreased) - G3b: 30–44 (Moderately to severely decreased) - G4: 15–29 (Severely decreased) - G5: < 15 (Kidney failure) Albuminuria Categories (UACR in mg/g): - A1: < 30 (Normal to mildly increased) - A2: 30–300 (Moderately increased, microalbuminuria) - A3: > 300 (Severely increased, macroalbuminuria) First-line pharmacotherapy for T2DM with CKD (eGFR 20-60 or UACR >= 30) includes an SGLT2 inhibitor and an ACE inhibitor or ARB (titrated to maximum tolerated dose). Nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (Finerenone) is recommended for persistent albuminuria.

chunks.title: Dyslipidemia Management and Cardiovascular Risk Reduction in T2DM
chunks.citation: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2024, Section 10
chunks.text: Dyslipidemia in T2DM is characteristically atherogenic: elevated plasma triglycerides, decreased HDL-C, and normal or mildly increased LDL-C consisting of small, dense LDL particles. Statin therapy guidelines: 1. Primary prevention (Age 40–75 without ASCVD): Moderate-intensity statin therapy (e.g., Atorvastatin 20 mg, Rosuvastatin 10 mg) recommended. In patients with multiple ASCVD risk factors, high-intensity statin is recommended to achieve an LDL-C reduction of >= 50% from baseline and LDL-C target < 70 mg/dL. 2. Secondary prevention (Established ASCVD): High-intensity statin therapy (Atorvastatin 40–80 mg, Rosuvastatin 20–40 mg) targeting LDL-C < 55 mg/dL. If LDL-C remains >= 55 mg/dL on maximally tolerated statin, add Ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor. Hypertriglyceridemia (fasting triglycerides >= 500 mg/dL) necessitates dietary intervention and consideration of fibrates or icosapent ethyl to prevent pancreatitis.

chunks.title: Clinical Follow-up Intervals and Decision Support Principles
chunks.citation: ADA Standards 2024, Section 4; WHO Package of Essential NCD Interventions 2023
chunks.text: Clinical visit frequency: Patients meeting treatment goals should be evaluated every 6 months. Patients not meeting treatment goals, or experiencing therapy modifications, adverse effects, or frequent hypoglycemia, should be reviewed every 3 months or sooner. Every clinical encounter must evaluate: 1. Glycemic trends (HbA1c, fasting/postprandial records). 2. Medication tolerance, reported adherence barriers, and adverse reactions. 3. Blood pressure measurement (target < 130/80 mmHg). 4. Symptomatic assessment of hypoglycemia, neuropathy, and volume status. Decision support rule: Clinical AI tools serve strictly as diagnostic and management aids for clinician review. All recommendations must present observed longitudinal evidence alongside guideline citations, without autonomous prescribing or dosing alterations.
